        sk_curr_group = VGroup(sk_curr_circle, sk_curr_label)

        sk_next_label = Text("SK_{t+1}", font_size=font_size_val)
        sk_next_group = VGroup(sk_next_circle, sk_next_label)

        # Arrange groups horizontally
        chain_vgroup = VGroup(sk_prev_group, sk_curr_group, sk_next_group)
        chain_vgroup.arrange(RIGHT, buff=1.5)

        # --- Create Connection Arrows ---
        arrow1 = Arrow(
            start=sk_prev_group.get_right(),
            end=sk_curr_group.get_left(),
            buff=0.15,
            color=WHITE,
            stroke_width=3
        )

            start=sk_curr_group.get_right(),
            end=sk_next_group.get_left(),
            buff=0.15,
            color=WHITE,
            stroke_width=3
        )

        # Group everything for the scene
        full_chain = VGroup(sk_prev_group, arrow1, sk_curr_group, arrow2, sk_next_group)
        full_chain.move_to(ORIGIN)

        # --- Animation Sequence ---
        # 1. Fade in the whole chain
        self.play(FadeIn(full_chain, shift=UP))

sections.title: The Privacy Dilemma
sections.content: Introduce the challenge of tracking virus spread without creating a 'Big Brother' surveillance state. Contrast Centralized vs. Decentralized approaches.
sections.example: Alice and Bob meet in a park. How can Bob be notified if Alice tests positive later, without a central server knowing exactly where they were or who they are?

sections.title: Prerequisite: Cryptographic Hash Functions
sections.content: Explain the concept of a one-way function (Hash). Use a visual of a 'meat grinder' where input goes in, but cannot be reconstructed from the output. Introduce the 'Seed' concept.
sections.example: Visualizing H(Key) = EphID. Even if a hacker sees the EphID, they cannot reverse-engineer the original Key.

sections.title: Step 1: Daily Key Generation
sections.content: Describe the hierarchical key structure. Each phone generates a random 'Secret Day Key' (SK) every 24 hours using a rotating sequence (SK_t = H(SK_{t-1})).
sections.example: Alice's phone generates a 'Monday Key'. From this key, it will derive many temporary IDs for that specific day.

sections.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Ephemeral IDs)
sections.content: Explain how the Day Key is used to produce Ephemeral IDs (EphIDs) that change every 15 minutes. These are broadcasted via Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE).
sections.example: While Alice sits in a cafe, her phone broadcasts 'ID_Alpha'. 15 minutes later, it broadcasts 'ID_Beta'. Bob's phone hears these and stores them locally.

sections.title: Step 3: The Encounter Log
sections.content: Focus on the decentralized storage. Every phone maintains a local 'diary' of observed EphIDs from others. No data is sent to the cloud yet.
sections.example: A visual split-screen showing Bob's phone storage filling up with a list of random strings from people he passed, labeled only with signal strength and duration.

sections.title: Step 4: Reporting and Notification
sections.content: When a user tests positive, they upload only their 'Secret Day Keys' for the infectious period to a public bulletin board. Other phones download these keys and 're-run' the math locally to see if they match any stored EphIDs.
sections.example: Alice tests positive. She uploads her 'Monday Key'. Bob's phone downloads it, generates the possible EphIDs from that key, and finds 'ID_Alpha' in its local diary. Bob gets a 'Risk Exposure' alert.

sections.title: Summary: Why it’s Secure
sections.content: Recap the three pillars: 1. No location data used. 2. Identities are pseudonymous. 3. Matching happens only on the user's device, not a server.
sections.example: An animation showing the 'Server' only holding a list of keys, while the 'Identity' and 'Location' of Alice and Bob remain locked inside their respective devices.

storyboard.title: Step 1: Daily Key Generation
lecture_lines: Each phone starts by generating a secret daily key.
This key changes automatically every twenty-four hours.
Today's key derives from the previous day's key.
This chain makes key management simple and secure.
These daily keys never leave your mobile device.
animations: A horizontal timeline labeled 'Days' appears on a phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg]. A node 'SK_t-1' (#00BFFF) is highlighted.
An arrow labeled 'Hash' connects 'SK_t-1' to a new node 'SK_t' (#FFD700).
Repeat the process to show 'SK_t+1' (#32CD32) appearing, forming a chain of daily keys.

storyboard.title: Step 2: The Digital Handshake (Ephemeral IDs)
lecture_lines: Daily keys generate multiple short-term ephemeral IDs.
These IDs rotate frequently, roughly every fifteen minutes.
Phones broadcast these random IDs via Bluetooth signals.
Nearby devices listen and collect these rotating IDs.
This handshake contains no personal or location data.
animations: Alice's phone icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] (#C0C0C0) emits a pulse ring (#00FF00) labeled 'EphID_1'.
A '15 min' timer icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/timer.svg] appears and completes a full rotation.

Alice's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] emits a new pulse ring (#FF00FF) labeled 'EphID_2'. Bob's phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] (#ADD8E6) enters and receives the pulse.

storyboard.title: Step 3: The Encounter Log
lecture_lines: Your phone keeps a private log of encountered IDs.
This log stays local and is never uploaded.
It only records proximity and duration of contact.
animations: A phone screen labeled 'Bob's Encounter Log' (#FFFFFF) is shown with empty rows.
Rows of text like 'ID: 4f2a...' and 'ID: 89b1...' appear one by one in light gray (#D3D3D3).
A 'Cloud' icon (#1E90FF) at the top is crossed out with a red slash to show no data leaves the device.

storyboard.title: Step 4: Reporting and Notification
lecture_lines: Infected users upload only their secret daily keys.
The central server hosts these keys for everyone.
Other phones download these keys to check exposure.
Devices locally reconstruct the IDs to find matches.
If a match exists, the user receives a notification.
animations: Alice's phone sends a 'Secret Day Key' (#00FFFF) to a 'Public Bulletin Board' (#F5F5F5) icon.
Bob's phone downloads the 'Secret Day Key' and many 'EphIDs' branch out from it using local computation.
One branched 'EphID' matches a row in Bob's 'Encounter Log'. The row turns red (#FF0000) and an alert pops up.

storyboard.title: Summary: Why it’s Secure
lecture_lines: DP-3T never uses or records your GPS location.
Your identity remains anonymous to the central server.
All sensitive matching happens locally on your phone.
animations: Three icons appear: 'No Location' (Map pin with X), 'Pseudonymous' (Mask), and 'Local Matching' (Phone [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] with gears).
A 'Server' icon [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/server.svg] (#808080) is shown holding only 'Keys' (#FFFFFF), isolated from user identities.
Final view: Two phones [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/phone.svg] (#C0C0C0) with a green checkmark (#00FF00) between them, signifying 'Privacy Preserved'.
